stem: A team puts NGINX in front of its application servers. Clients connect only to NGINX, which forwards each request to one of the app servers and returns the response. What is this component called, and what does it hide from clients?
explanation: A reverse proxy terminates client connections on behalf of a group of servers. That single entry point is where TLS termination, compression, caching, load balancing and path-based routing usually live, and backends can be added or replaced without clients noticing.

options.text: A reverse proxy: it acts on behalf of the servers, so clients never see the individual backends
options.why: A reverse proxy sits on the server side and presents one address for many backends.

options.text: A forward proxy: it acts on behalf of the clients and hides their identities and addresses from servers
options.why: A forward proxy sits on the client side, like a corporate egress proxy, and hides clients rather than servers.

options.text: A NAT gateway: it rewrites outbound source addresses so that private instances can reach the internet
options.why: NAT handles outbound connections from private hosts; it does not terminate and route inbound HTTP requests.

options.text: A service mesh: it injects a proxy beside every client process and routes calls between internal services
options.why: A mesh puts a sidecar next to each service for internal traffic, not one shared entry point for external clients.

stem: A team moves its site to a new IP address by updating its DNS A record, which had a TTL of 86,400 seconds. An hour later, many users still reach the old server. Why?
explanation: The TTL tells every recursive resolver and client how long it may cache an answer. Before a planned move, lower the TTL (for example to 60 seconds) at least one old-TTL period in advance, then change the record, and keep the old server running until its traffic drains away.

options.text: Resolvers and clients may keep using the cached old record until its one-day TTL runs out
options.why: Each cache may hold an answer for up to the TTL it received, so changes spread slowly with long TTLs.

options.text: DNS changes are published to the root servers only once a day, during a fixed global update window
options.why: There is no global window: the authoritative server serves the new record at once, and caches expire on their own.

options.text: Browsers pin the IP address of every site they have visited until the user clears the browsing history
options.why: Browsers cache DNS only briefly (often about a minute), and history has nothing to do with it.

options.text: The old server keeps answering because HTTP keep-alive connections never close once they are opened
options.why: Keep-alive connections close on idle timeouts; the lasting effect here is cached DNS answers living for a day.

stem: A web app serves its JavaScript bundles, images and fonts from its own servers in one region. Users on other continents see slow page loads. What is the main benefit of serving these files through a CDN?
explanation: Static assets are the easiest CDN win: they are the same for every user and change only on deploy. Use content-hashed file names (such as `app.3f9c1.js`) with a long `Cache-Control: max-age` and `immutable`, so each deploy publishes new URLs instead of needing cache purges.

options.text: The CDN compresses every file far more than the origin could, so each download becomes much smaller for users
options.why: CDNs can compress, but so can origins; distance and origin load are the main gains.

options.text: Copies are cached at edge sites near users, so most requests avoid the long trip and never reach the origin
options.why: Shorter round trips cut latency, and cache hits take load off the origin.

options.text: The CDN replaces the origin entirely, so the application servers no longer need to keep these files
options.why: The origin still holds the master copy; edges fetch from it on a miss or after expiry.

options.text: Browsers download all the files over a single UDP stream from the CDN, which removes handshake costs
options.why: Some CDNs offer HTTP/3 over QUIC, but that is a protocol detail, not the core benefit of a CDN.

stem: Adding read replicas to a single-leader PostgreSQL setup increases the number of writes per second the database can accept.
explanation: Read replicas spread read traffic, but with single-leader replication every write goes through the leader, and each replica must apply it too. To scale writes you shard the data across several leaders, reduce write volume (batching, fewer indexes), or use a store designed for many writers.

options.text: True
options.why: Every write still goes to the one leader, and each replica must replay every write as well.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: replicas scale reads only; write throughput is limited by the single leader.

stem: A DNS provider announces the same IP address from 200 data centres worldwide. A user in Mumbai and a user in Paris both send queries to that one address. What makes each query reach a nearby data centre?
explanation: Anycast advertises one IP prefix from many locations, and BGP delivers each packet to the closest one in routing terms (usually, but not always, the closest geographically). It is the standard way to run DNS and CDN edges, and it absorbs DDoS floods by spreading them across many sites.

options.text: GeoDNS: the provider looks up the country of each user and returns the address of their nearest site
options.why: GeoDNS hands out different addresses per location; here everyone uses one address.

options.text: Anycast: BGP routing delivers packets for the shared address to the nearest site that announces it
options.why: With anycast, the network itself chooses among the many sites announcing one prefix.

options.text: Multicast: each packet is copied to all 200 data centres, and the first one to respond wins the race
options.why: Multicast delivers to a group of receivers; it would multiply load and is not used this way on the internet.

options.text: Round-robin DNS: each user gets the next address from a list, which spreads users evenly across sites
options.why: Round robin rotates among several addresses and ignores distance; here there is only one address.

stem: Load tests show one instance of a stateless API handles 500 requests per second at its target utilization. Peak traffic is 12,000 requests per second, and the team keeps 2 extra instances so that losing any two still covers the peak. How many instances should run at peak? Type a number.
explanation: 12,000 ÷ 500 = 24 instances carry the peak at target utilization. Adding 2 spares (N+2) gives 26, so the fleet still meets the peak when two instances fail or are being replaced during a deploy.

stem: Match each component with the job it does in a scaled-out web system.
explanation: Each piece removes a different coupling. The gateway hides the internal layout from clients, the registry lets instances come and go, the sidecar moves network concerns out of application code, and the CDN keeps static traffic away from the origin. A message broker decouples producers from consumers in time, which none of these four jobs describes.

options.text: API gateway
Service registry
Sidecar proxy
CDN edge
Message broker

prompts.text: The single public entry point that authenticates requests, applies rate limits and routes them to internal services
Keeps a live list of healthy instances so that callers can find where a service is running
Runs next to each service instance and handles its outbound calls, retries and mutual TLS
Serves cached static files from a location close to the user

stem: A load balancer opens a new TCP and TLS connection to a backend for every single request. Which two benefits would reusing persistent (keep-alive) connections to the backends bring? (Choose two.)

options.text: Lower latency, because requests skip the TCP and TLS handshakes
options.why: Each new connection costs at least one round trip for TCP and more for TLS before any data flows.

options.text: Less CPU spent on TLS handshakes and fewer sockets left in TIME_WAIT
options.why: Handshakes are CPU-heavy, and churning connections can exhaust ephemeral ports.

options.text: Even load across backends no matter how long each connection lives
options.why: Long-lived connections can make load less even, which is why balancers spread requests per request, not per connection.

options.text: Backends can keep per-user session state in memory without any risk
options.why: Connection reuse is per balancer, not per user, so it gives no session affinity.

options.text: Requests no longer need timeouts, because the connection is already open
options.why: Persistent connections still need idle and request timeouts on both sides.

explanation: Connection reuse (HTTP keep-alive, connection pools, HTTP/2 multiplexing) removes per-request setup. That saves round trips, TLS CPU and ephemeral ports. The trade-off is that long-lived connections can unbalance load and must be drained on deploys, so balancers pool connections but still choose a backend per request.

stem: A team keeps upgrading its single database server to larger machines. Which is the main limitation of relying only on this vertical scaling?
explanation: Scaling up is often the right first move because it needs no code changes. But machine sizes have a ceiling, the price per unit of capacity rises near the top, resizing can mean downtime, and one server is still one failure domain. Horizontal scaling (replicas, sharding) removes those limits at the cost of distribution complexity.

options.text: There is a ceiling on machine size, and the one server remains a single point of failure
options.why: Hardware tops out, costs rise steeply near the top, and one box can still fail.

options.text: Larger machines cannot run the same database software, so the application must be rewritten each time
options.why: The same software runs on bigger hardware; that is what makes vertical scaling simple.

options.text: Vertical scaling only adds disk space and never adds CPU or memory to the database server at all
options.why: Scaling up adds CPU, memory, disk and network together; that is its definition.

options.text: Each upgrade splits the data across more machines, which forces the team to choose a shard key early
options.why: Splitting data across machines is horizontal scaling (sharding), not vertical scaling.

stem: An app replaces server-side sessions with stateless JWT access tokens valid for 24 hours, so that any instance can verify a request without a session store. Security now asks that "Log out of all devices" and account suspension take effect within a minute. What is the standard way to meet that?
explanation: A self-contained token can't be recalled before it expires. Trade a little statelessness for control: issue access tokens for 5–15 minutes, require refresh tokens that are checked against a store and rotated on use, and keep a small deny-list of revoked token IDs (or a per-user "valid after" timestamp) for emergencies.
reference: OWASP JSON Web Token Cheat Sheet

options.text: Sign every token with its own per-user key, then delete that user's key on the server at logout
options.why: Per-user keys need a lookup on every request, which is a session store by another name.

options.text: Use short-lived access tokens and refresh tokens checked against a store, plus a deny-list for urgent cases
options.why: Short expiry bounds exposure; the refresh check and a small deny-list give central, fast revocation.

options.text: Have the browser delete the token from local storage, which immediately invalidates every copy of it
options.why: Deleting one copy does nothing to copies on other devices or held by an attacker.

options.text: Lengthen the token lifetime to 30 days so that fewer tokens are issued and fewer need revoking
options.why: Longer lifetimes widen the window in which a stolen or revoked token still works.

stem: Workers pull image-resize jobs from a queue. Each job mostly waits on a slow external API, so worker CPU stays below 20% even when thousands of jobs are waiting and customers complain about delays. Which two signals are best for autoscaling this pool? (Choose two.)
explanation: Scale on the signal that reflects the work, not on a resource the work doesn't use. For queue consumers that is backlog per worker, with a target set from how many jobs one worker clears within the latency goal, plus oldest-message age as a guard. AWS documents exactly this "backlog per instance" metric for SQS-based scaling.
reference: AWS docs: Scaling based on Amazon SQS

options.text: Waiting jobs divided by the current number of workers (backlog per worker)
options.why: Backlog per worker grows the pool in step with the work actually queued.

options.text: Age of the oldest job still waiting in the queue
options.why: Oldest-job age tracks the delay customers feel and also catches a stalled pool.

options.text: Average CPU utilization across the workers
options.why: The workers are I/O-bound, so CPU stays low however large the backlog grows.

options.text: Memory used by each worker process
options.why: Memory does not rise with queue depth for this kind of worker, so it never triggers scaling.

options.text: Number of jobs the whole pool completes per minute
options.why: Throughput alone can't tell a quiet period from a saturated pool with a growing backlog.

stem: An autoscaling group of 10 instances adds one instance when average CPU is above 60% and removes one when it is below 55%, checking every 60 seconds. With steady traffic, it keeps adding and removing instances every few minutes, and each new instance needs 3 minutes to warm up. What is the best fix?
explanation: Removing one of N instances raises average CPU by N ÷ (N − 1). At 10 instances and 54% CPU, removing one gives 54 × 10 ÷ 9 = 60%, which triggers a scale-out again. Leave a band wider than one instance's effect, scale in slowly (a stabilization window longer than warm-up), or use target tracking, which builds this in.

options.text: Check CPU every 10 seconds instead of every 60, so that the group reacts more quickly to every change
options.why: Faster checks make the oscillation faster, not smaller.

options.text: Widen the gap between the two thresholds and add a scale-in stabilization window longer than warm-up
options.why: Hysteresis plus a cool-down stops one instance's change from pushing the metric across the other threshold.

options.text: Scale on memory instead of CPU, because memory usage changes more slowly and smoothly than CPU does
options.why: A different metric with the same narrow band can flap just the same, and memory may not track load.

options.text: Raise the thresholds to 90% and 85% so that the group runs hotter and therefore scales less often
options.why: This keeps the same narrow band, removes headroom for spikes and still flaps.

stem: A gRPC service runs behind a layer-4 (TCP) load balancer. Each client opens one HTTP/2 connection and sends all its calls over it. After the service scales from 4 to 12 instances during a spike, the 8 new instances get almost no traffic while the original 4 stay overloaded. Why?
explanation: An L4 balancer makes one decision per connection. HTTP/2 and gRPC reuse a connection for thousands of calls, so a scale-out only helps clients that reconnect. Fix it with an L7 proxy that balances each call (Envoy, Linkerd, a gRPC-aware balancer), client-side balancing across several subchannels, or a server-side maximum connection age that makes clients reconnect periodically.

options.text: The L4 balancer picks a backend per TCP connection, and the clients' long-lived connections stay on the original instances
options.why: HTTP/2 multiplexes every call over one connection, so balancing per connection means balancing per client.

options.text: New instances must pass health checks for 30 minutes before any load balancer will route traffic to them
options.why: Health checks take seconds, not 30 minutes; the new instances are healthy but get no new connections.

options.text: gRPC refuses to send calls to instances that it has not contacted before, as a security precaution
options.why: gRPC has no such rule; it sends calls on whatever connections it has open.

options.text: The balancer uses round robin, which always favours the instances that were registered first in the pool
options.why: Round robin rotates evenly among registered backends; the problem is that clients open no new connections.

stem: A browser looks up `api.example.com` for the first time, and no cache along the way has an answer. Put the lookup steps in order.
explanation: Any step can be skipped by a cache hit: in the browser, the OS, the recursive resolver, or its cached referrals for the root and `.com` zones. That layered caching is why DNS scales, and it is also why record changes spread no faster than their TTLs allow.

options.text: The browser asks the operating system's stub resolver
The stub resolver sends the query to a recursive resolver, such as the ISP's or a public one
The recursive resolver asks a root server, which refers it to the `.com` servers
The recursive resolver asks a `.com` server, which refers it to example.com's authoritative servers
The authoritative server returns the record, and the recursive resolver caches it for its TTL

stem: A function-as-a-service API idles overnight. At 9:00, traffic jumps from almost nothing to 300 concurrent requests in a few seconds. p50 latency stays at 40 ms, but p99 reaches 3 seconds for the first few minutes. The function loads a large framework and opens a database connection when it starts. What causes the p99 spike, and what reduces it most directly?
explanation: Each concurrent request needs its own instance, so a burst of 300 creates hundreds of new instances, each paying for runtime start, code loading and connection setup. Keep some capacity warm (provisioned concurrency, minimum instances), trim or defer heavy initialisation, and reuse connections across invocations.

options.text: The database is overloaded by the morning traffic, so adding read replicas will bring the p99 latency back down
options.why: p50 is unaffected, which points at per-instance start-up rather than a database bottleneck.

options.text: Cold starts: new instances must start and initialise first; pre-warmed capacity and lighter init cut this
options.why: Requests landing on brand-new instances pay the start-up cost; requests on warm ones don't.

options.text: The platform throttles every function at 9:00 each day to protect other customers from sudden spikes
options.why: Throttling shows up as 429 errors, not as a slow tail that fades once instances are warm.

options.text: Network routes are recomputed every morning, which delays the first packets of every new connection
options.why: Routing does not reset daily; the delay matches instance initialisation.

stem: A 15-engineer startup plans to split its monolith into 20 microservices. Which three are real costs the split will add? (Choose three.)
explanation: Microservices trade in-process simplicity for independent deployability. For a small team the costs (network failures, distributed data, API versioning, more infrastructure, harder debugging) often outweigh the benefits. A well-modularised monolith is usually the better start, with services carved out where scaling needs or team boundaries demand it.

options.text: In-process function calls become network calls that can be slow, fail or time out
options.why: Every remote call adds latency and failure modes that need timeouts and retries.

options.text: Changes that span several services need coordinated releases and versioned APIs
options.why: Cross-service changes need backward-compatible contracts and staged rollouts.

options.text: An operation that used one database transaction may now need a saga or a similar pattern
options.why: Splitting the data across services loses local ACID transactions.

options.text: Each service can be deployed and scaled on its own schedule
options.why: That is a benefit, and the main reason teams adopt microservices.

options.text: Teams can choose a language and data store that suit each service
options.why: Per-service technology choice is a benefit (with an operational price), not the cost asked about.

options.text: A bug in one module can no longer crash the whole process
options.why: Fault isolation is a benefit, not a cost.

stem: A chat app's WebSockets pass through a cloud load balancer with a 60-second idle timeout. Users in quiet rooms are disconnected about a minute after the last message, while users in busy rooms stay connected. What is the best fix?
explanation: Load balancers, proxies and NAT devices drop connections that carry no data for a while. Heartbeats shorter than the smallest idle timeout keep quiet connections alive, and missed heartbeats let both sides notice a dead link quickly and reconnect with backoff.

options.text: Switch the balancer to round robin so that each user's connection moves to a new server every minute
options.why: An open WebSocket is one TCP connection; the algorithm only matters when connections are opened.

options.text: Raise the balancer's idle timeout to 24 hours and send no traffic at all on quiet connections in the meantime
options.why: Very long timeouts leave dead connections hanging, and NATs and proxies on the path have their own timeouts.

options.text: Send WebSocket ping frames or app heartbeats every 20–30 seconds, below every idle timeout on the path
options.why: Regular small frames keep the connection active and also detect dead peers.

options.text: Have the client open a new WebSocket for every message it sends and close it straight afterwards
options.why: That throws away the persistent connection that makes WebSockets worth using.

stem: Putting a CDN in front of an API reduces origin load for responses marked `Cache-Control: private`, because the CDN can serve each user's cached copy from the edge.
explanation: RFC 9111 defines `private` as "only a private cache, such as the browser, may store this". A CDN can still help that traffic by terminating TLS near users and keeping warm connections to the origin, but it won't serve those responses from cache. To offload personalised pages, split them into a shared, cacheable shell plus small per-user API calls.

options.text: True
options.why: `private` tells shared caches such as CDNs not to store the response; only the user's own browser may.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: a shared cache must not store a private response, so each request still goes to the origin.

stem: Every API instance's load-balancer health check runs `SELECT 1` against the shared database and fails if it takes over 500 ms. One evening a heavy batch job slows the database to 800 ms per query. Within a minute the balancer marks every instance unhealthy, and the site returns errors to all users, even for pages that never touch the database. What design change prevents this?
explanation: A health check that includes a shared dependency turns one dependency problem into a fleet-wide removal: every instance fails together. Check what the balancer can act on (is this process up and able to serve?) and let the application deal with slow dependencies by timing out, serving cached or partial content, or shedding load. Some balancers "fail open" when all targets are unhealthy, but you should not depend on it.
reference: AWS Builders' Library: Implementing health checks

options.text: Raise the health-check timeout from 500 ms to 5 seconds so that slow database answers stop counting as failures
options.why: That only moves the threshold; a worse slowdown would still remove the whole fleet at once.

options.text: Keep the balancer's check about the instance itself, and handle a slow dependency inside the app
options.why: A shared dependency failing should not make every healthy instance look broken at the same moment.

options.text: Add more API instances, so the balancer always has enough healthy ones left to send traffic to
options.why: Every new instance checks the same slow database and fails in the same way.

options.text: Run the health check only every 5 minutes, so that brief database slowdowns are never noticed by it
options.why: Rare checks delay detection of real instance failures and still fail during a long slowdown.

stem: A company fails over from region A to region B by changing its API's DNS record, which has a 60-second TTL. Ten minutes later browsers have all moved to B, but one partner's long-running Java service is still sending requests to region A's dead address. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: DNS failover is only as fast as the slowest cache. The JVM keeps its own address cache (`networkaddress.cache.ttl`), which caches forever when a security manager is installed and defaults to 30 seconds otherwise, and HTTP clients or connection pools can pin addresses too. For critical failover, prefer anycast or a global load balancer that keeps the IP address fixed.

options.text: The partner's JVM keeps its own cache of DNS answers, possibly forever, and ignores the record's TTL
options.why: Some JVM setups cache resolved addresses indefinitely unless `networkaddress.cache.ttl` is set.

options.text: DNS TTLs apply only to browsers, so server processes keep their first DNS answer until they are restarted
options.why: Resolvers and most server runtimes honour TTLs; the JVM's own cache policy is the exception here.

options.text: Region B's new address has not reached the root DNS servers yet, so some resolvers still return A
options.why: Root servers don't hold your records; the authoritative servers returned B's address straight away.

options.text: The 60-second TTL is counted from midnight each day, so the change takes effect only on the next day
options.why: TTLs count from when each cache received the answer, not from a fixed time of day.

stem: A user-profile service runs active-active in two regions. Both regions accept writes, and their databases replicate to each other asynchronously with last-writer-wins on whole rows. Users who travel sometimes see a profile change revert a few seconds after saving it. Which two changes address the cause? (Choose two.)
explanation: With asynchronous multi-leader replication, two regions can accept conflicting writes to the same row, and last-writer-wins throws one away, which users see as a revert. Either avoid conflicts (a single home region per user or key, with failover) or make them mergeable (field-level merges, CRDTs). Faster links only narrow the window.

options.text: Give each user a home region that takes all their writes, and route writes there
options.why: One writer per record removes concurrent cross-region conflicts.

options.text: Merge concurrent updates per field (for example with CRDTs) instead of overwriting whole rows
options.why: A defined merge keeps both changes instead of silently discarding one.

options.text: Raise the bandwidth between the regions so that conflicting writes can no longer happen
options.why: Faster replication shrinks the window, but concurrent writes in two regions still conflict.

options.text: Use GeoDNS so that each request goes to the region nearest the user at that moment
options.why: That is what sends a travelling user's writes to two regions in the first place.

options.text: Add read replicas in each region so that reads are always served locally
options.why: The problem is conflicting writes, not read capacity or read latency.

stem: An API keeps instances at a 60% CPU target, and one instance handles 1,000 requests per second at 100%. It runs 17 instances for a steady 10,000 requests per second. A marketing push will raise traffic to 25,000 requests per second within 2 minutes at 18:00, and a new instance takes 5 minutes to become ready. What should the team do?
explanation: Reactive autoscaling can only add capacity as fast as instances start. 17 instances max out at 17,000 req/s, so a 2-minute ramp to 25,000 overloads them for several minutes. For known events, scale on a schedule: 25,000 ÷ (1,000 × 0.6) ≈ 41.7, so about 42 instances, ready before the ramp. Predictive scaling and warm pools serve the same purpose for recurring patterns.
reference: AWS docs: Scheduled scaling for Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling

options.text: Nothing: target-tracking autoscaling will add instances as CPU rises and can keep up with the spike
options.why: With a 5-minute start-up, capacity lags a 2-minute ramp, and 17 instances top out at 17,000 req/s.

options.text: Lower the CPU target to 40% at 18:00 so that autoscaling responds more aggressively to the spike
options.why: A more sensitive target still waits 5 minutes for every new instance to become ready.

options.text: Scale ahead: have about 42 instances ready before 18:00 (25,000 ÷ 600), then let autoscaling take over
options.why: Pre-scaling to the planned peak at target utilisation covers the ramp.

options.text: Double the fleet to 34 instances at 18:00, which gives twice today's capacity for the coming spike
options.why: 34 × 600 = 20,400 req/s at target, short of 25,000, and they would not be ready until 18:05.

stem: Six API instances sit behind a load balancer that uses "least outstanding requests". After a bad config push, one instance loses its database credentials and starts returning HTTP 500 in 2 ms, while healthy instances take about 80 ms per request. Its TCP health check still passes. What happens to the error rate, and what prevents it?
explanation: Load-aware algorithms reward whoever finishes requests fastest, and nothing is faster than failing. The broken instance can end up with most of the traffic (a "black hole"). Defend with health checks that test the ability to serve, passive outlier detection that ejects backends whose 5xx rate jumps (Envoy outlier detection, NGINX `max_fails`), and alerts on per-instance error rates.

options.text: About one sixth of requests fail, because the balancer keeps spreading requests evenly across all six
options.why: Least-request balancing is not even when one backend finishes far faster than the rest.

options.text: Far more than a sixth fail, because the fast-failing instance has the fewest requests in flight; eject outliers by error rate
options.why: Fast failures look like spare capacity; outlier detection on 5xx rates removes the bad instance.

options.text: No requests fail, because the balancer retries every 500 response on a different healthy instance
options.why: Balancers don't retry non-idempotent requests by default, and many never retry a 500.

options.text: Errors stay low, because the TCP health check will remove the broken instance within a few seconds
options.why: A TCP check only tests that the port accepts connections, which it still does.

stem: To keep each user on the same server, a load balancer hashes the client IP address to pick one of 10 backends. After a large enterprise customer onboards, one backend runs at 95% CPU while the others sit near 30%. The customer's 8,000 employees all reach the service through one corporate proxy. What explains this, and what is the better approach?
explanation: Source-IP affinity treats everyone behind a NAT or proxy (offices, mobile carriers, universities) as one client. When affinity is really needed, key it on something per user, such as a balancer-set cookie or a session or user ID, and prefer making the service stateless so any instance can serve any request.

options.text: The hash function is weak; switching from MD5 to MurmurHash would spread the customer evenly across servers
options.why: Any hash maps one IP address to one backend; the input has no variety to spread.

options.text: The backends have uneven hardware; replacing the overloaded server with a faster one will rebalance it
options.why: The load follows the customer, so a faster machine only postpones the problem.

options.text: All 8,000 users share one source IP and land on one backend; use a cookie or session key, or drop affinity
options.why: A finer-grained key spreads the users again, and stateless backends need no affinity at all.

options.text: IP hashing needs a power-of-two number of backends, so running 8 or 16 servers would even out the load
options.why: Hash-mod works for any backend count; the problem is that one key carries 8,000 users.

stem: Match each symptom seen while scaling a web service with its most likely cause.

options.text: Database connection pool exhaustion
options.why: Requests queue for a connection while CPU stays idle.

options.text: A hot key or sticky routing
options.why: Traffic can't spread, so one instance saturates.

options.text: Lock contention on shared state
options.why: Extra instances just wait on the same lock.

options.text: Cold caches and JIT warm-up on new instances
options.why: New instances are slow until they warm up.

prompts.text: p99 latency climbs while app CPU sits at 30%, and request threads are waiting on `getConnection()`
One instance is pinned at 100% CPU while the other 19 are nearly idle
Throughput stays flat as instances go from 8 to 16, and database lock-wait time doubles
Every scale-out event brings a short latency spike that fades after a few minutes

explanation: Scaling problems tend to have distinct signatures. Low CPU with high latency means requests are waiting on something, often a pool or a downstream dependency. One hot instance means load can't be spread. Flat throughput as you add nodes means contention. A spike after each scale-out that fades means new capacity is cold, which is why slow start and pre-warming exist.

stem: A PostgreSQL server allows `max_connections = 800`, and 50 of those are reserved for admin tools, replication and migrations. Each API instance keeps a pool of 25 connections. What is the largest number of API instances the autoscaler may run before new instances can't open their pools? Type a number.
explanation: (800 − 50) ÷ 25 = 30 instances. The cap is easy to hit during a spike or a rolling deploy, which briefly runs old and new instances side by side. Common fixes are a connection pooler such as PgBouncer in transaction mode, smaller per-instance pools, and setting the autoscaler's maximum from this calculation.

stem: A notification service holds 2 million WebSockets across 40 servers. During a rolling deploy, each server is drained by closing all its connections at once. Every client reconnects immediately to the remaining servers, and each wave of TLS handshakes and session reloads pushes their CPU to 100%, sometimes failing health checks. What is the best fix?
explanation: Each server holds 2,000,000 ÷ 40 = 50,000 connections, so dropping them at once sends a 50,000-client reconnect burst at the other 39 servers, once per server deployed. Drain over minutes (close connections in batches or send a "reconnect later" message), add jitter to client reconnects, and make reconnects cheap (TLS session resumption, lightweight re-authentication).
reference: AWS Builders' Library: Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter

options.text: Deploy all 40 servers at the same moment, so that clients only have to reconnect once instead of in waves
options.why: All 2 million clients would then reconnect together, the worst possible storm.

options.text: Close connections gradually during the drain, and make clients reconnect after random, jittered delays
options.why: Spreading closes and reconnects over time keeps the handshake rate within capacity.

options.text: Use a smaller TLS key size so that each reconnect handshake costs much less CPU on the receiving servers
options.why: Weakening security for a load problem is the wrong trade, and the burst is still unbounded.

options.text: Raise the health-check failure threshold so that busy servers are not removed while reconnects arrive
options.why: That hides the overload rather than avoiding it, and users still see slow or failed reconnects.

stem: A network load balancer has nodes in two availability zones, and DNS spreads clients evenly across the two nodes. Zone A has 2 backend instances and zone B has 8. Cross-zone load balancing is disabled, so each node sends traffic only to instances in its own zone. What share of total traffic does each zone-A instance receive, compared with each zone-B instance?
explanation: With cross-zone balancing off, traffic is split evenly per zone first (50/50), then per instance inside each zone: 50% ÷ 2 = 25% and 50% ÷ 8 = 6.25%. Each zone-A instance carries 4× the load of a zone-B instance. Fix it by enabling cross-zone balancing (which can add inter-zone data charges) or by keeping instance counts equal per zone, as autoscaling groups do by default.
reference: AWS ELB docs: Cross-zone load balancing

options.text: 10% each, the same as every zone-B instance, because traffic is always spread evenly across all 10 instances
options.why: That is what happens with cross-zone balancing turned on, not off.

options.text: 25% each, against 6.25% for each zone-B instance, because every zone gets half of all traffic
options.why: Half the traffic over 2 instances is 25% each; half over 8 is 6.25% each.

options.text: 50% each, because each node sends all its traffic to a single instance in its zone at any one time
options.why: Each node still balances across all the healthy instances in its own zone.

options.text: About 20% each, because traffic is weighted by the instance count of each zone and then rounded up
options.why: Without cross-zone balancing there is no weighting by instance count; each zone gets an equal half.

stem: A service runs active-active in two regions. Each serves half of global traffic and runs at 70% of its capacity. The team wants to survive the loss of either region without overload, and is considering adding a third region. Which two statements are correct? (Choose two.)
explanation: To survive one region failing with N equal regions, each must run at no more than (N − 1) ÷ N of its capacity, because the survivors split the lost region's load. Two regions allow 50%, three about 66.7%, four 75%. More regions make spare capacity cheaper, which is one reason large services run in several regions rather than two.

options.text: Today, losing one region sends 140% of a region's capacity to the survivor, so it overloads
options.why: The survivor takes both halves: 2 × 70% = 140% of its capacity.

options.text: With three equal regions, each can run at up to about 66% and the two survivors absorb a failure
options.why: Survivors carry 1.5× their normal load, and 66% × 1.5 ≈ 100%.

options.text: Two regions can each safely run at 70%, because autoscaling adds the missing capacity instantly
options.why: Autoscaling takes minutes and may hit quotas during a regional outage.

options.text: A third region doesn't change how hot each region may run; the limit is always 50% per region
options.why: The safe level is (N − 1) ÷ N: 50% for two regions, about 67% for three, 75% for four.

options.text: Two regions at 70% are safe as long as the DNS TTL moves traffic within one minute
options.why: Moving traffic faster just overloads the survivor sooner.

stem: A company serves large downloads, some lasting over an hour, from an anycast IP address announced at 30 edge sites. Short web requests work well, but some long downloads fail midway with connection resets, and the failures cluster at times when the network team changes BGP routes. What explains this?
explanation: Anycast is stable for most traffic because routes rarely change during a short connection. Long-lived flows are exposed to route changes and shifting equal-cost paths. Operators mitigate it by keeping routing stable, forwarding packets for unknown connections to the site that owns them, or serving long transfers in ranged chunks (or from a unicast address handed out by the first anycast request).
reference: RFC 7094: Architectural Considerations of IP Anycast

options.text: Anycast sprays each connection's packets across every site at once, so long transfers collect corrupted data
options.why: Routing follows paths, not per-packet spraying; a flow's packets take one route until it changes.

options.text: A route change moves the connection's packets to another site, which has no state for it and resets it
options.why: TCP state lives on one server; a new site sees packets for an unknown connection and replies with RST.

options.text: BGP route changes flush DNS resolver caches, so clients look the name up again and connect to a new address
options.why: BGP and DNS are separate systems, and the anycast address stays the same.

options.text: Long downloads exceed the maximum TCP window, which anycast networks cannot negotiate with clients
options.why: Window scaling is negotiated end to end and is unrelated to how routes are announced.

stem: A load balancer uses consistent hashing on video ID to send requests to 20 cache servers, so that each video stays cached on one server. One video goes viral and takes 30% of all requests. Its server falls over, then the next server on the ring takes the video and falls over too. Which change keeps most of the cache affinity while preventing this?
explanation: Plain consistent hashing gives affinity but no load guarantee: a hot key lands on one server, and when that server fails the key cascades along the ring. Consistent hashing with bounded loads (Mirrokni, Thorup and Zadimoghaddam), available in HAProxy as `hash-balance-factor` and used by Vimeo for video caching, caps each server at c times the average and overflows to the next server. Replicating very hot keys is the other common answer.
reference: Mirrokni et al., Consistent Hashing with Bounded Loads (2018)

options.text: Switch to plain round robin so that every server receives exactly the same share of the requests
options.why: Round robin balances perfectly but discards affinity, so every server must cache every video.

options.text: Add many more virtual nodes for each server on the ring, which spreads that single viral video across more servers
options.why: Virtual nodes even out how keys are spread, but one key still maps to one server.

options.text: Use consistent hashing with bounded loads: a server over a cap, such as 1.25 × average, overflows to the next
options.why: The cap keeps every server out of overload while nearly all keys still land on their home server.

options.text: Hash on the video ID plus the current second, so that the viral video moves to a new server every second
options.why: That defeats caching: every server keeps fetching the video and nothing stays hot.

stem: A function-as-a-service handler serves 2,000 requests per second, each taking 300 ms, mostly waiting on PostgreSQL. Each function instance handles one request at a time and opens its own database connection. The database allows 500 connections. Traffic is steady, yet the database keeps rejecting connections. What is the root cause, and the best fix?
explanation: Concurrency = arrival rate × duration = 2,000 × 0.3 = 600 instances, each holding a connection, which exceeds 500 even at steady state. Serverless scales by adding instances, so it multiplies connections. Put a connection pooler (RDS Proxy, PgBouncer) between the functions and the database, cap the function's concurrency at what the database can take, and keep queries short.
reference: AWS docs: Using Amazon RDS Proxy with Lambda

options.text: The memory setting is too low; doubling it adds CPU, so requests finish fast enough to free connections
options.why: More CPU barely helps I/O-bound requests, and concurrency stays well above 500.

options.text: The platform's concurrency limit is too low; raising it lets more instances run and clears the errors
options.why: More instances means more database connections, which makes the rejections worse.

options.text: About 600 instances run at once (2,000 × 0.3 s), each holding a connection; add a pooling proxy and cap concurrency
options.why: Concurrency is 600 against 500 connections, and a pooler multiplexes many callers onto fewer connections.

options.text: The database needs read replicas, which would spread these queries out and remove the need for more connections
options.why: Replicas only help read queries, each has its own connection limit, and the fan-in problem remains.

stem: A CDN uses GeoDNS to send users to their nearest edge. Users in Jakarta who use a large public DNS resolver are routed to an edge in Tokyo, while users there on their ISP's resolver reach the Jakarta edge. What explains this, and what fixes it?
explanation: DNS-based geo-routing only sees the IP address of the recursive resolver that asks, and a public resolver may query from a site far from the user. EDNS Client Subnet (RFC 7871) lets the resolver pass a truncated client subnet, so the authoritative server can answer for the user's network. Anycast routing avoids the problem because it routes on the user's own packets.
reference: RFC 7871: Client Subnet in DNS Queries

options.text: GeoDNS sees the resolver's location, not the user's; EDNS Client Subnet sends the user's subnet so the answer fits
options.why: With ECS, the authoritative server sees part of the client's address and picks a nearby edge.

options.text: Public resolvers ignore TTLs, so they keep returning the Tokyo edge long after the CDN switched its routing to Jakarta
options.why: Large public resolvers honour TTLs; the issue is which location the answer is computed for.

options.text: The Jakarta edge is out of capacity, so the CDN deliberately sends users of public resolvers to Tokyo
options.why: Nothing points to capacity: users on ISP resolvers are served from Jakarta without trouble.

options.text: Anycast sends these users' packets to Tokyo, so switching the CDN from anycast to GeoDNS would fix it
options.why: The CDN already uses GeoDNS; the wrong edge is chosen before any data packet is routed.

stem: A gRPC server (HTTP/2) must be taken out of service without failing in-flight or new calls. Clients hold long-lived connections to it through client-side load balancing. Which two steps belong to a correct graceful shutdown? (Choose two.)
explanation: HTTP/2 has graceful shutdown built in: a GOAWAY frame with the last processed stream ID tells clients which calls were accepted and to open new ones elsewhere, and the server finishes those streams before closing. gRPC servers expose this as a graceful stop. Pair it with removing the instance from service discovery first, and a hard deadline so a stuck stream can't block the deploy forever.

options.text: Send an HTTP/2 GOAWAY frame so that clients stop opening new streams on this connection
options.why: GOAWAY names the last stream the server will process, so clients send new calls elsewhere.

options.text: Keep serving streams already in progress until they finish or a drain deadline passes, then close
options.why: Letting in-flight calls complete avoids failing them midway.

options.text: Close the TCP socket at once, since clients retry every failed call automatically
options.why: Not every call is safe to retry, and an abrupt close fails every in-flight call.

options.text: Stop answering health checks but keep accepting new streams until the process exits
options.why: Clients on existing connections keep sending calls, which are cut off at exit.

options.text: Send RST_STREAM on every open stream so that clients resend those calls elsewhere
options.why: RST_STREAM cancels calls in progress, exactly what a graceful drain should avoid.

stem: A service runs active-passive: region A is primary, and region B holds an asynchronously replicated database replica. Region A is badly degraded but still partly reachable. Put the failover steps in the order that avoids split-brain writes.
explanation: Fence first: if region A can still write while B is promoted, both accept writes and the data diverges (split brain). Then measure what replication had not delivered, promote B, and only then send traffic to it. Writes that only reached A must be reconciled before A rejoins as a replica, or they are silently lost.

options.text: Fence region A so it can no longer write (revoke its database credentials or block its write path)
Check region B's replication lag and record which recent writes may be lost
Promote region B's replica to be the new primary
Move traffic to region B with a DNS, global load balancer or anycast change
Once region A recovers, reconcile its unreplicated writes before making it a replica of B
